title: Merge sort, LCS and Kruskal's MST
overview: Three classic algorithms close the course. Merge sort shows divide and conquer: split the array in half, sort each half, merge them. Longest common subsequence is a two-string DP. Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by taking the cheapest edges that do not form a cycle, using DSU. The module's quiz material also contrasts substrings with subsequences.

concepts.explain: Break the problem into halves, solve each half recursively, then combine. For merge sort the combining step is the merge.
Keep one pointer in each array, copy the smaller front element, advance that pointer, and finally copy whatever is left.
log n levels of halving, and each level does O(n) merge work, so O(n log n) time with O(n) extra memory.
A substring is a contiguous block of characters. A subsequence keeps the order but may skip characters. `ace` is a subsequence of `abcde`, not a substring.
Compare the last characters: equal gives 1 + lcs of both shorter strings; different gives the better of dropping one character from either string.
concepts.snippet:
if (a[i] == b[j]) return 1 + lcs(i-1, j-1);
return max(lcs(i-1, j), lcs(i, j-1));

concepts.explain: A set of n-1 edges that connects all nodes with the smallest total weight and no cycle.
Sort edges by weight. Walk through them and keep an edge only if its ends are in different DSU groups; then union them.

files.title: Merge two sorted arrays
files.what: The 'conquer' half of merge sort on its own: merges two sorted arrays into one sorted array with two pointers.
steps: Read sizes `n`, `m` and the two sorted arrays `a`, `b`.
`i`, `j` point into `a`, `b`; `curr` points into the result `c`.
While both have elements, copy the smaller front element into `c` and advance.
Copy the rest of whichever array is not finished.
Print `c`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: n m, then the two arrays, each already sorted.
files.output_note: Prints `1 2 3 4 7 8 9`: every element of both arrays, in order.
files.watch_out: The inputs must already be sorted; merging unsorted arrays gives an unsorted result.

check.q: How many comparisons can merging 4 and 3 elements need at most?
check.a: 6 (n + m - 1), because each comparison places one element and the last one needs no comparison.

files.title: The divide step (splitting only)
files.what: Shows the recursive splitting of merge sort without the merge. It reads an array and halves the range until single elements remain, but prints nothing.
steps: `divide(a, l, r)` stops when `l >= r` (one element or none).
Otherwise `mid = (l + r) / 2`.
Recurse on the left half `[l, mid]` and the right half `[mid+1, r]`.
`main` reads `n m` (m is not used) and the array, then calls `divide(a, 0, n-1)`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) calls · Space O(log n) recursion depth
files.input_note: n and an unused m, then n values.
files.output_note: No output: this file only demonstrates the splitting. Add a `cout << l << " " << r << endl;` at the top of `divide` to watch the ranges.

check.q: For n = 8, how many levels of splitting are there before ranges have size 1?

files.title: Merge sort
files.what: Combines both halves: `divide` sorts the left and right halves recursively and `conquer` merges them back into the original array.
steps: `divide(a, l, r)`: return if the range has one element.
Sort `[l, mid]` and `[mid+1, r]` recursively.
`conquer` copies the two halves into temporary arrays `a` and `b`.
It merges them back into `c[l..r]` with the two-pointer method.
`main` prints the sorted array.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n and an unused m, then n values (a duplicate 5 is included).
files.watch_out: `main` still reads an unused `m`, left over from `conquer.cpp`; the input must contain it. Using `a[i] <= b[j]` in the merge would make the sort stable (equal values keep their order).

check.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n), even on already-sorted input?
check.a: It always splits in the middle and always merges, whatever the order of the values.

files.title: Longest common subsequence (memoized)
files.what: Finds the length of the longest subsequence shared by two strings, using `lcs(i, j)` on prefixes `a[0..i]` and `b[0..j]` with a memo table.
steps: `memset(dp, -1, ...)` and read strings `a`, `b`.
Base case: an empty prefix (`i < 0` or `j < 0`) gives 0.
If `a[i] == b[j]`, the answer is `lcs(i-1, j-1) + 1`.
Otherwise the best of skipping `a[i]` or skipping `b[j]`.
Print `lcs(n-1, m-1)`.
files.watch_out: The top comment says 'substring', but the code computes the longest common **subsequence**; a substring version would reset to 0 when characters differ. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What is the LCS length of `abc` and `def`?

files.title: Minimum spanning tree with Kruskal
files.what: Sorts all edges by weight and greedily keeps each edge that joins two different DSU groups. The sum of kept weights is the MST cost.
steps: Read the edges into `edge_list` as `Edge(a, b, c)`.
`sort` them with `cmp`, cheapest first.
For each edge, find the leaders of both ends.
Different leaders: `dsu_union` them and add the weight to `total_cost`.
Same leader: skip it, it would form a cycle.
Print `total_cost`.
files.complexity: Time O(E log E) · Space O(n + E)
files.input_note: n e, then e edges `a b weight`.
files.output_note: The program crashes before printing anything (status `exit_0xc0000005`, an access violation), and the compiler warns `no return statement in function returning non-void`. That missing `return` is the cause (see Watch out). With the fix it prints `6`: edges 1-2 (1), 3-4 (2) and 1-3 (3).
files.watch_out: `dsu_union` is declared to return `int` but never returns anything. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, and here it makes the program crash on the first union. Make it `void dsu_union(...)`. Also, `memset(group_size, 1, ...)` fills bytes, not ints; set sizes with a loop. If the graph may be disconnected, also count kept edges and check that there are n-1. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`.

check.q: Why is it safe to skip an edge whose ends already share a leader?
check.a: Its ends are already connected by cheaper (or equal) edges, so adding it would only create a cycle and raise the cost.

recap: Merge sort = split in half, sort both halves, merge with two pointers: O(n log n).
Substring is contiguous; subsequence keeps order but may skip characters.
LCS: equal last characters add 1; otherwise take the better of dropping one side.
Kruskal = sort edges + DSU; keep an edge only when it joins two groups.
An MST of n nodes has exactly n-1 edges.

check_yourself.q: What is the longest common subsequence of `ABCBDAB` and `BDCABA`, in length?
How many substrings does a string of length 4 have (counting repeats)?
Why does Kruskal need the edges sorted?
check_yourself.a: The greedy rule 'always take the cheapest safe edge' only gives the minimum total if edges are considered from cheapest to most expensive.
